claims.claim: Fluid and electrolyte balance is the body's regulation of water and dissolved minerals (electrolytes) within the fluid compartments inside and outside cells; the amount of water taken in should equal the amount lost.
Electrolytes are minerals that carry an electric charge (positive or negative) when dissolved in water or body fluids, including blood.
Sodium is the most abundant electrolyte outside cells; it helps control the amount of fluid in the body and supports nerve and muscle function.
Potassium is the most abundant electrolyte inside cells; it helps cells, the heart, and muscles work properly and helps regulate heart rhythm.
Calcium helps make and keep bones and teeth strong and is needed for muscle contractions, nerve impulses, and blood clotting.
Chloride helps control the amount of fluid in the body and helps maintain healthy blood volume and blood pressure.

About two-thirds of body fluid is inside the cells (intracellular fluid) and about one-third is outside the cells (extracellular fluid); the extracellular fluid includes interstitial fluid and blood plasma (intravascular fluid).
Water accounts for about 60 percent of an adult's body weight.

Total body fluid is regulated by the renal system: the kidneys retain or release water and electrolytes, guided by hormones including antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and aldosterone, and thirst signals the body's need for water.

Dehydration is the condition of losing more fluid than the body takes in, so the body does not have enough fluid to work properly; common causes include vomiting, diarrhea, fever with heavy sweating, and inadequate intake.

Fluid volume overload (hypervolemia) is the retention of an excessive amount of fluid, commonly associated with heart failure, kidney failure, and cirrhosis; an electrolyte imbalance means one or more electrolyte levels are too low or too high.

Even slight abnormalities in electrolyte levels can have serious consequences, and when homeostasis fails the body is at risk of organ dysfunction — the clinical reason nurses monitor fluid and electrolyte status closely.

positions: MedlinePlus uses 'dehydration' for losing more fluid than the body takes in
OpenStax treats 'fluid volume deficit', 'hypovolemia', and 'dehydration' as overlapping names for the same condition
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches dehydration as the everyday term and notes that clinicians also call it fluid volume deficit or hypovolemia; both sources agree on the mechanism (fluid loss exceeds intake).

conflictingEvidence.issue: How reliable thirst is as a signal
positions: Thirst is listed among the symptoms of dehydration (MedlinePlus)
Some older adults lose their sense of thirst, so it is not a reliable early warning in everyone (MedlinePlus)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents thirst as the body's signal that water is low while noting the older-adult caveat, matching MedlinePlus exactly.
